b.v: Today's goal

v: Understand the difference between ebook and paperback
Know what print on demand means
Decide what you will publish first

b.v: About 15 minutes. Read this before you write a single page.

KDP stands for Kindle Direct Publishing. It is Amazon's service that lets an individual publish a book and sell it on Amazon without an agent or a publisher. You upload a file, they list it, and when someone buys, they print or deliver it and pay you a royalty.
1) The two main formats
You can publish the same book in more than one format, but each has its own file and its own rules. Start with one.

v: Ebook: a digital file read on a phone or Kindle, no printing, no stock
Paperback: printed only when someone orders, which is print on demand
Hardback: limited to certain sizes and page counts
Audiobook: a separate service, not needed on day one

b.v: 2) What print on demand means
You never buy 500 copies and store them in your bedroom. When an order comes, Amazon prints one copy and ships it. Your printing cost is taken out of the sale, and the rest is your royalty.

v: No upfront printing bill
No stock and no storage
Printing cost depends on page count, size and ink type
You cannot sign or personally ship copies easily

b.v: Do not pay someone who promises guaranteed sales or a bestseller badge. Nobody can guarantee sales, and these offers usually target new authors.
3) What you get and what you do not
KDP gives you distribution and printing. It does not give you readers, reviews or a marketing budget.

v: You get: a listing on Amazon marketplaces, printing, delivery, payment collection
You get: a sales dashboard and monthly reports
You do not get: editing, cover design or promotion included
You do not get: control over Amazon's storefront layout

b.v: Practice
Open the KDP website and read the help page on paperback printing cost. Write down the three things that change the printing cost of your idea.
Today's goal

v: Understand what a royalty really is
Know why ebook and paperback royalties differ
Learn to read the current rate table yourself

b.v: About 20 minutes. Open the KDP pricing page while you read.

A royalty is your share of a sale. It is not a fixed salary, and it is not the same as profit, because tax and any costs you paid yourself still come out of it. The percentages change over time and differ by format and marketplace, so this lesson teaches the logic, not the digits.
1) Ebook royalty, in simple logic
For ebooks there are usually two royalty options, and one pays much more per sale but comes with price limits and a delivery charge based on file size.

v: Higher rate option: better per sale, but only inside an allowed price band
Lower rate option: available at almost any price, and outside that band
A delivery cost is deducted on the higher rate option, based on file size
Big images make the file bigger, so they reduce your royalty

b.v: 2) Paperback royalty, in simple logic
For paperbacks the printing cost is subtracted first, then your percentage applies. That is why page count and trim size matter so much.

v: Royalty = selling price minus printing cost, multiplied by the rate
More pages means a higher printing cost and a lower royalty
Black ink on cream paper is cheaper to print than colour
Large trim sizes cost more than standard ones

b.v: Do not set a price before you check the printing cost for your exact page count. A 300 page book and a 90 page book cannot share the same price and both make money.
3) Read the table, do not memorise numbers
Amazon publishes a royalty and printing cost table per marketplace. It is the only source you should trust, and it is updated without announcement.

Check rates properly:|Open the KDP help page for royalty options|Find your format and your marketplace|Note the allowed price band for the higher rate|Open the printing cost page and enter your page count|Write the numbers in your notebook with today's date|Repeat this check before every new book
Practice
Take a 120 page black ink paperback at a standard size. Find today's printing cost for it, then calculate what you would receive at two different selling prices.

day-3.t: Day 3 — Low content or a real guide book

b.v: Today's goal

v: Know the difference between low content and guide books
Pick the lane that matches your time and skills
Avoid the categories that are already flooded

b.v: About 15 minutes. Be honest about how much time you have.

Low content books are mostly blank: notebooks, planners, journals, logbooks, colouring pages. Guide books contain real writing that teaches something. They need very different amounts of work, and they sell in very different ways.
1) Low content, honestly described
Low content is fast to produce and heavily competed. A plain lined notebook with a nice cover sells occasionally. A notebook for a very specific use sells better.

v: Fast: a cover plus an interior template
Cheap: no editing needed
Hard: thousands of near identical books already exist
Works when it targets a narrow use, like a monthly expense log for a small shop

b.v: 2) Guide books, honestly described
A guide book is the better long term asset because it can rank for real questions and earn reviews. It also takes weeks, not hours.

v: Slower: real writing, real structure
Needs editing, even a friend's honest read helps
Ranks for specific problems people search
Builds your name, which helps the next book

b.v: Do not publish a low content book with a misleading title that suggests it contains information. Buyers report it, refunds rise, and the account gets flagged.
3) Choose for your situation
There is no single right answer. Match the format to your hours, your knowledge and your patience.

v: Two hours a week and no writing habit: start with one focused low content book
You know a trade well: write a short practical guide
You want a catalogue: low content in series, one cover style
You want one strong asset: one good guide, well edited

b.v: Practice
Write one sentence: my first book is a ____ for ____. Then write why a stranger would pay for it instead of searching online for free.

day-4.t: Day 4 — Choose a topic people search for

b.v: Today's goal

v: Find topics with real demand and weak competition
Use free research instead of paid tools
Write a one page book plan

b.v: About 25 minutes. Use the Amazon search bar itself.

A book nobody searches for cannot sell, no matter how good it is. Research is not about finding a magic niche. It is about finding a question people already type into Amazon, where the existing books are weak.
1) Free research routine
The Amazon search bar suggests what real people type. That is free demand data, updated constantly.

Research a topic:|Type a broad word into Amazon and note the autocomplete suggestions|Pick one suggestion and search it|Look at the first page: how many reviews do the top books have|Read the three star reviews for complaints about gaps|Write the exact phrase people use, not your own wording
2) Judge the competition honestly
You are looking for a gap, not an empty shelf. A category with no books often has no buyers.

v: Strong signal: top books have reviews, but the newest ones are weak
Weak signal: the whole first page is famous books with thousands of reviews
Weak signal: no book at all on the exact topic
Look for specific readers: a trade, a city, a language, a life stage

b.v: Do not write about a topic only because it is popular if you cannot answer the reader's real questions. Thin books get one star reviews and stop selling within weeks.
3) Write the one page plan
Before writing, decide the reader, the promise and the length. One page saves a month of drifting.

v: Reader: exactly who this is for
Promise: what they can do after reading
Length: a short guide of 60 to 120 pages is enough
Difference: what the existing books miss

b.v: Practice
Do the search routine for three topics and note the review counts on the first page. Pick the one with real demand and the weakest top listing, and write its one page plan.

day-5.t: Day 5 — Outline, then write in small pieces

b.v: Today's goal

v: Build a chapter outline before writing prose
Write one chapter in one sitting
Keep your own voice and avoid copied text

b.v: About 25 minutes. Write badly first, fix later.
Most unfinished books die because the writer started at page one with no map. An outline is a list of questions your reader has, in the order they have them. Then each chapter answers one.
1) Outline as questions
Turn the reader's journey into questions. Each heading becomes a chapter, and the answer becomes the page.

Build the outline:|List ten questions your reader would ask|Group them into four to eight chapters|Order them from beginner to advanced|Add one practice task at the end of every chapter|Cut any chapter that does not help the promise
2) Write in 25 minute blocks
A book is written in small sessions, not in one heroic weekend. Two hundred words a day finishes a short guide in a few months.

v: One chapter per session, no editing while writing
Use your own examples from your city or job
Say the idea out loud first, then type it
Stop mid sentence so tomorrow is easy to start

b.v: Never paste text from a website, a translated article or another book. It is easy to detect, it breaks copyright, and Amazon removes books and closes accounts for it.
3) Edit in one pass, then stop
Endless editing delays publishing. Two passes are enough for a short practical guide.

v: Pass one: cut anything that does not help the reader
Pass two: read aloud and fix sentences that trip you
Ask one honest reader for the confusing parts
Check every fact you are unsure about, or remove it

b.v: Practice
Write your ten questions and group them into chapters today. Then write 200 words of chapter one, badly, and stop.

day-6.t: Day 6 — Cover basics that look professional

b.v: Today's goal

v: Understand what makes a cover work at thumbnail size
Build a simple cover with free tools
Get the technical requirements right

b.v: About 25 minutes. Free design tools are enough.
The cover is your only advertisement on a results page. It appears as a small thumbnail next to twenty others, so it is judged in under a second. Pretty is not the goal. Clear is the goal.
1) Design for the thumbnail
Zoom out to phone size and look at your draft. If you cannot read the title, nothing else matters.

v: Title readable at thumbnail size, two or three words per line
One strong image, not five small ones
High contrast between text and background
Genre signals: readers expect a certain look per category

b.v: 2) Build it with free tools
You do not need Photoshop. A free design tool with the right dimensions produces a clean cover.

Make the cover:|Check the current KDP cover size and file requirements in help|Create a canvas at that size with the correct resolution|Place one image or a bold colour block|Add the title in a readable font, then the subtitle|Add the author name at the bottom|Export as the file type KDP asks for, under the size limit|View it at thumbnail size before uploading
Do not use a random image from Google. You need a licence for every image. Use your own photo or a site that clearly grants commercial use, and keep the licence note.
3) The back cover and spine
For paperbacks the back cover is part of the same file. It holds the blurb and a barcode area that the printer adds.

v: Leave the barcode area clear, the printer places it there
Blurb: three short paragraphs, the last one a promise
Spine text only if the page count allows it
Check the previewer, it shows every alignment error

b.v: Practice
Make one cover draft today and view it at phone thumbnail size. If the title is not readable, change the font size before anything else.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Format the inside so it passes

b.v: Today's goal

v: Set up a document with the right page size and margins
Add the front and back matter a book needs
Upload and use the previewer properly

b.v: About 25 minutes. A word processor is enough, no special software.
Formatting problems are the main reason a first upload gets rejected. The rules are boring and exact: page size, margins, fonts, and no automatic page numbers in the wrong place.
1) Set the page before typing
Changing page size after writing ruins every layout. Set it first, then write or paste.

Set up the file:|Choose a standard trim size in the KDP help page|Set the page size to match exactly|Set inside margin larger than outside, for the binding|Choose one readable serif font at 11 or 12 points|Set line spacing to about 1.15 to 1.5|Add page numbers starting after the front matter
2) The pages around the book
Front and back matter make the file feel like a real book and give the reader somewhere to go next.

v: Title page, then copyright page with your name and year
Table of contents, linked if it is an ebook
Chapters starting on a new page
About the author and one link at the end
No page numbers on blank pages

b.v: Do not paste text with double spaces, manual line breaks and mixed fonts. It looks fine on your screen and messy in the printed copy, and the previewer will show it.
3) Upload and check the previewer
The previewer is a free proof copy. Use it before you press publish, and again after any change.

v: Check the first page and the last page
Check a middle chapter for headers and page numbers
Check that no text is cut at the margins
Check the ebook version separately, it reflows

b.v: Practice
Format three chapters today using the correct trim size and margins, then open the previewer and fix every warning it shows.

day-8.t: Day 8 — Keywords, categories and the description

b.v: Today's goal

v: Fill the keyword fields with real search phrases
Choose categories that fit the book
Write a description that converts

b.v: About 20 minutes. Have your research notes open.
Amazon decides who sees your book using your title, subtitle, keywords and categories. Getting these right is free advertising. Getting them wrong hides a good book in a corner nobody visits.
1) Keywords are search phrases
You have a limited number of keyword fields. Each one should be a phrase a real buyer would type, not a single word and not a repetition of your title.

v: Use phrases of two to four words
Cover different angles: problem, reader, format, occasion
Do not repeat words already in the title
No competitor names, no other authors, no misleading words

b.v: 2) Categories
A category is a shelf. Choosing three accurate ones puts the book where browsing readers look.

Choose categories:|Open the KDP category list or the store browse tree|Find two or three shelves that truly match the content|Avoid the most crowded shelf unless your book fits it exactly|Check what the top books in that shelf look like|Update later if the book is not being found
Do not stuff the title with keywords to game search. Titles that do not read like titles get rejected, and readers distrust them.
3) The description
The description is sales copy, not a summary. It should speak to the reader's problem in the first two lines, because only those lines show before the read more link.

v: Line one: the reader's problem, in their words
Line two: what the book helps them do
Then four to six short benefit lines
Then who it is for, and who it is not for
End with one clear next step

b.v: Practice
Write seven keyword phrases and three categories for your book. Then write the first two lines of the description and read them aloud.

day-9.t: Day 9 — Pricing, marketplaces and reviews policy

b.v: Today's goal

v: Set a price using the royalty logic
Understand why prices differ by marketplace
Learn the review rules before you ask anyone

b.v: About 20 minutes. Check the current rate table again.

Price is not a guess. For each marketplace the royalty rate, the printing cost and the currency are different, so the same number in dollars and rupees does not give the same income. Work each marketplace separately.
1) Set the ebook price
Low prices sell more copies but earn less each. For a first book, a modest price inside the higher royalty band usually makes sense.

v: Check the current allowed band for the higher royalty rate
Price inside the band to earn the better rate
Keep the file small so any delivery cost stays low
Change the price later, it is not permanent

b.v: 2) Set the paperback price
Here the printing cost sets your floor. Anything below it loses money on every sale.

Price it safely:|Find the printing cost for your page count and ink type|Write your floor price above that cost|Compare with three similar books in your category|Pick a price that is fair to the reader and profitable to you|Repeat for each marketplace in its own currency
Do not set a paperback price below the printing cost by mistake. Amazon will not pay you a negative royalty, and the book simply cannot go live at that price.
3) The review rules
Reviews are the most abused part of publishing. Amazon's policy forbids paying for reviews, swapping reviews, and asking family to post them. Breaking it risks the book and the account.

v: Never pay for a review, in cash or in gifts
Never ask friends or family to review your book
Never review your own book from another account
You may ask readers to leave an honest review, with no incentive

b.v: Practice
Calculate your paperback floor price for two marketplaces using today's printing costs. Write both numbers with the date next to them.

day-10.t: Day 10 — Payments, tax and keeping the account open

b.v: Today's goal

v: Set up payment and tax details correctly from Pakistan
Know the pitfalls that close accounts
Publish your first book and check the listing

b.v: About 25 minutes. Do this with your bank details in front of you.
This is the lesson that protects months of work. Payment details and tax forms are boring until they block a payout, and account closures almost always come from a rule broken weeks earlier.
1) Payment and tax for a seller in Pakistan

Amazon pays royalties by bank transfer to accounts in supported countries. For a seller in Pakistan the usual route is through a service that gives you a receiving account in a supported country, and you complete the tax interview as a non US person.

Set it up carefully:|Open the KDP tax interview and answer honestly as an individual or business|Complete the form for non US persons, which usually reduces withholding|Add bank details exactly as printed on the account|Confirm the name matches your tax details|Wait for verification before publishing a lot of books|Keep a copy of every form you submit
Do not use someone else's bank account or a name that does not match your tax details. Mismatches freeze payouts and are very slow to fix.
2) The pitfalls that close accounts
Most closures are not dramatic. They are repeated small violations that trip an automated check.

v: Copied content, including translated or lightly rewritten text
Public domain text re-uploaded as your own work
Multiple accounts for the same person without permission
Manipulating reviews or rankings
Titles and covers that mislead about the contents
Uploading the same book many times with tiny changes

b.v: 3) Publish and verify
The last step is the easiest to rush. Check the live listing the way a buyer would.

v: Search your exact title and find the book
Check the cover, price, description and categories on the live page
Buy one copy of your own paperback to inspect the print
Fix anything wrong before you tell anyone about it

b.v: Practice
Finish the tax interview and payment details today, then write your publishing checklist on one page: file, cover, keywords, categories, price, preview checked.
